relations.note: Duttur is Dumuzi’s mother in the pastoral genealogy.
She seeks or grieves for Dumuzi after anticipating his death.
Some incantatory and learned traditions identify Enki as Dumuzi’s father.
A distinct cowherd or royal genealogy associates Ninsun maternally with Dumuzi.
Geštinanna is Dumuzi’s sister, protector, interpreter, and fellow netherworld substitute.
She explains that each dream omen predicts his capture and death.

relations.myth: Geštinanna conceals Dumuzi from the galla
relations.note: She endures torture without disclosing her brother’s hiding place.
Geštinanna spends part of each year in the netherworld in Dumuzi’s place.
Akkadian and learned traditions describe Belili as Dumuzi’s sister or female mourner.
Learned tradition sometimes equates Belili with Dumuzi’s sister Geštinanna.
Inanna is Dumuzi’s lover, bride, or wife across love poetry and royal ideology.
Dumuzi woos and sleeps with Inanna, bringing abundance and royal legitimacy.

relations.myth: Inanna chooses between shepherd and farmer
relations.note: Dumuzi competes for Inanna’s favor after she initially prefers Enkimdu.
Finding him enthroned and splendidly dressed, Inanna orders the galla to seize him.

relations.myth: Inanna laments and decrees alternating absence
relations.note: She later laments Dumuzi and participates in assigning the siblings alternating half-years below.
Gilgamesh says Ištar ordained yearly wailing for Dumuzi, lover of her youth.
Tammuz is washed, anointed, clothed, and accompanied by music; his relation to Ištar remains disputed.
Utu advocates his shepherd brother-in-law’s wealth over the farmer Enkimdu’s produce.
Utu changes Dumuzi’s body so he can temporarily flee the pursuing galla.
Dumuzi invokes Utu for metamorphoses, but the demons repeatedly discover him.
Utu transforms Dumuzi so he can escape and seek refuge with his sister.

relations.myth: Shepherd and farmer compete for Inanna
relations.note: Dumuzi challenges Enkimdu by matching agricultural products with his pastoral goods.
Enkimdu yields and offers produce; Dumuzi reciprocates with milk and cheese.

relations.myth: Bilulu blamed for Dumuzi’s desert death
relations.note: A regional tradition blames Bilulu for his death, prompting Inanna’s vengeance.
Bilulu’s son is implicated in Dumuzi’s death and consequently punished by Inanna.

relations.myth: Dumuzi and Ning̃išzida guard Anu’s gate
relations.note: The vanished gods jointly favor Adapa and speak on his behalf before Anu.
Dumuzi stands at Anu’s gate and intercedes favorably for Adapa.
Seleucid Uruk theologians included Dumuzi in a learned equation with Anu.
Seleucid Uruk theology equated Dumuzi with Enmešarra and Anu.
An initially independent divine name was absorbed into Dumuzi’s identity.
Laments and god lists assimilate the two young disappearing gods despite their distinct origins.
Hellenistic and Roman interpreters associated Adonis with Tammuz through analogous death and mourning traditions.

relations.myth: Galla pursue Dumuzi as Inanna’s substitute
relations.note: The netherworld demons chase, bind, and seize Dumuzi after Inanna surrenders him.

relations.myth: Galla capture and kill the fugitive shepherd
relations.note: Despite repeated escapes and transformations, the demons beat, bind, and kill or drag Dumuzi below.

relations.myth: Galla torture Geštinanna and find Dumuzi
relations.note: The demons hunt Dumuzi, torture his sister, and eventually find him at the sheepfold.
